title: Pipkin and Lulu's Great Card Rescue
markdown:
Dawn broke in gold and pink. Pipkin the squirrel did not merely wake. He exploded from his oak nest, tail a fluffy question mark, eyes already scanning the park. Dewy grass. Cool air. Zing. Branch to branch.

“Today feels extra special,” he chattered.

Below, Lulu the guinea pig shook sleep from her chocolate fur. Her nose wiggled. She blinked. Then there was Pipkin, a whirlwind against the sky.

“Pipkin,” she squeaked. “It is so wonderfully bright.”

“Spectacular,” Pipkin sang, jigging. “An adventure is brewing. I can feel it in my whiskers.”

A bright blue card fluttered down and landed with a soft thump. Pipkin, always quickest, snatched it.

“Park Library Card. Property of Mrs. Gable.”

Lulu’s ears perked. “The librarian. She needs that. The book cart leaves soon.”

Pipkin’s heart did a flip-flop. Mrs. Gable wheeled the colourful cart. Today it went to Whispering Woods. Without the card, stories would sit stacked and stuck.

“Less than an hour,” Pipkin said. His paws itched to zip off alone, a brown rocket with no waiting.

Lulu planted herself in the path, round and sure. “We can do it. Together. Not just fast.”

Pipkin’s tail flicked. He grinned anyway. “Not quick enough if we stop to nibble dandelions. This is our park-tastic parade of purpose.”

He became a blur down the oak. Lulu took a breath and trotted, paws pumping. “Wait for me, Pipkin,” she puffed.

They dashed past the daisy patch, dewdrops catching the first gold. Pipkin leapt over a fat caterpillar. “Excuse me, sir.” Lulu navigated around it, polite as a librarian herself, round body wobbling but determined.

“The pond,” Pipkin pointed. Mrs. Gable loved the lily pads, and the morning still smelled of wet stones and possibility.

They skidded. No Mrs. Gable. Near bright red toadstools sat a tiny picnic basket, and peeking out, a familiar fluffy grey hat.

“She was here,” Lulu panted. “She must have dropped the card when she packed.”

The path to the cart was a good sprint. Pipkin scrambled over gnarled roots, tail a banner of speed. A breeze shook the trees. Crack. A pinecone bounced near Lulu.

“Whoa,” she squeaked.

Pipkin had already rounded the bend. The cart wheels began to creak. Mrs. Gable patted her pockets, flustered. This was the ordeal, and it had his name on it: go now, be the fastest, leave Lulu in the pine-needles.

He skidded. He came back. They went around the final bend together.

“Mrs. Gable,” they shouted.

She turned, surprised, then delighted. “Pipkin. Lulu. What a wonderful morning greeting.”

Pipkin held up the blue card. “We found this. We thought you might need it.”

Mrs. Gable gasped. “My library card. Just in time. You have saved the day. The Whispering Woods adventure can absolutely begin.”

She slid the card into her pocket. The cart let out a happy whee as she steered toward the rustling trees. They had spent their whole bright hour on the dash. That was the cost, and it sat in Pipkin’s chest like a fair trade.

They watched from the same oak-shadow where dawn had found them. Tails wagging. Noses wiggling.

“We made it,” Lulu beamed, catching her breath.

Pipkin grinned, but he did not puff quite so high. He looked at Lulu first, then at the wide park. He waited until her paws were ready.

“Today,” he declared, eyes sparkling, “is going to be amazing.”
